title: Stable pairings and deferred acceptance
sections: Take two disjoint sets of n objects, each with a complete strict ranking of the other side. A perfect matching is stable if no unmatched opposite-side pair both prefer one another to their assigned partners. A one-sided wish is not a blocking pair.

Deferred acceptance: A free proposer asks its highest-ranked unasked receiver. Each receiver holds its favorite proposal so far and rejects the rest; holds can change. No proposal repeats, so at most n² occur. With equal sides and complete lists, the process finishes with a perfect stable matching.

The key invariant is that a receiver’s held choice can only improve. If a proposer preferred another receiver to its final partner, it must have asked there earlier and been rejected; that receiver finishes with someone it prefers. Hence the alleged pair cannot block.

Optional stronger theorem: For a fixed proposing side, every proposer receives its best partner among all stable matchings. The outcome is independent of the order in which free proposers act. Reversing the proposing side can change it. Stability need not be unique, give everyone a first choice, or maximize total satisfaction. These statements assume complete strict lists and equal finite sides; do not extend them unchanged to ties or omitted choices.
In a stable three-pair matching, at most three of the six objects can receive their last choice. This bound is attainable; stability limits mutual dissatisfaction without eliminating it.
K–1: An optional two-pair investigation, only after the child can check that both sides prefer a switch. An adult reading the strips cannot replace that logical gate.
Grades 2–3: Find all stable pairings in small profiles and construct preference lists with specified outcomes.
Grades 4–5: Track proposals and temporary holds, compare the proposing sides, and prove termination and stability.

The launch contrasts one-sided and mutual wishes. Running several profiles tests a conjecture; the nonrepeating-proposal and improving-hold arguments prove the universal guarantee. The original readiness gate and longer proof keys follow.
